html:
The Rwandan genocide was the mass killing of Tutsi in Rwanda by Hutu extremists over about a hundred days, from April to July 1994. Estimates of the dead run from about 500,000 to 800,000 or more, most of them Tutsi, along with Hutu who opposed the killing and many Twa.

Its roots lay partly in colonial rule. Belgian administrators treated Hutu and Tutsi as fixed races and put the label on identity cards. Independence in 1962 brought a Hutu-led republic and waves of violence that drove many Tutsi abroad. In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front, formed by Tutsi exiles, invaded from Uganda.

On 6 April 1994 the plane carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down over Kigali. Within hours, soldiers and the Interahamwe militias began killing from prepared lists, at roadblocks, in churches and in schools, urged on by radio broadcasts. Neighbours killed neighbours, mostly with machetes. The small UN force was cut back, and the world held back from calling it genocide.

The killing ended as the RPF under Paul Kagame took the country in July. About two million Hutu, among them many killers, fled into Zaire and Tanzania, starting the Great Lakes refugee crisis and later the Congo wars. Leaders were tried by the international tribunal at Arusha, and hundreds of thousands of others by the village gacaca courts.
